source.title: Jaynes–Cummings Model and a Non–Commutative “Geometry” : A Few Problems Noted

accepted.question_text: For classical field models that admit non-commutative versions, why should one construct and study those non-commutative versions, and what mathematical or physical advantage does such a generalization provide over the original classical model?
accepted.context_brief: Motivation for non-commutative classical field models

evidence.quote: Why do we consider non–commutative versions of classical field models ? What is an advantage to consider such a generalization ?
Researchers in this subject should answer such natural questions. This note may give one of answers.

accepted.question_text: Can the classical Hopf bundles over the real numbers, complex numbers, quaternions, and octonions be generalized to non-commutative versions in a way that is mathematically or physically meaningful, given that local descriptions of the classical Hopf bundles encounter singular lines called Dirac strings?

evidence.quote: The Hopf bundles (which are famous examples of fiber bundles) over K = R, C, H (the field of quaternion numbers), O (the field of octanion numbers) are classical objects and they are never written down in a local manner. If we write them locally then we are forced to encounter singular lines called the Dirac strings, see [1].

We would like to make the Hopf bundles non–commutative. Whether such a generalization is meaningful or not is not clear at the current time, however it may be worth trying, see for example [5] or more recently [6] and its references.

accepted.question_text: For classical models with singular objects such as singular points or singular lines, can one find many examples in which passing to a non-commutative model makes those singularities milder or removes them partly, and can one construct a general theory explaining when this removal or mitigation occurs?
accepted.context_brief: General theory of singularity removal under non-commutativization

evidence.quote: It is probable that a non–commutative model makes singular objects (singular points or singular lines or etc) in the corresponding classical model mild or removes them partly.

More generally, it is probable that a singularity (singularities) in some classical model is (are) removed in the process of non–commutativization. Further study on both finding many examples and constructing a general theory will be required.
